candidate.answerReason: Removing the 21 trailing zeros gives an integer congruent to 12 modulo 25 and divisible by 4, so its last two digits are 12.

methods.label: Remove the zeros and find small remainders
methods.explanation:
A trailing zero comes from a factor of \(10=2\cdot5\), so first count the factors of \(5\) in \(90!\). There are \(18\) multiples of \(5\), and \(25,50,75\) each contribute one additional factor of \(5\). Thus there are exactly \(21\) factors of \(5\). The \(45\) even numbers already supply at least \(45\) factors of \(2\), so there are exactly \(21\) trailing zeros.

After removing those zeros, let
\[
M=\frac{90!}{10^{21}}.
\]
At least \(45-21=24\) factors of \(2\) remain, so \(M\) is divisible by \(4\). We will also find its remainder upon division by \(25\). The notation \(a\equiv b\pmod{25}\) means that \(a-b\) is divisible by \(25\).

For a positive integer \(m\), let \(P(m)\) be the product of the integers from \(1\) through \(m\) that are not divisible by \(5\). The multiples of \(5\) in \(90!\) have product \(5^{18}18!\). Applying the same observation to \(18!\) gives
\[
90!=P(90)5^{18}18!
=5^{21}P(90)P(18)3!.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{21}M=P(90)P(18)\cdot6.
\]
This identity removes every factor of \(5\), making the remaining products easier to reduce.

Group the factors of \(P(m)\) into blocks of the form \(5k+1,5k+2,5k+3,5k+4\), where \(k\) is a nonnegative integer. Pairing the outside factors and the inside factors gives
\[
(5k+1)(5k+4)=25k(k+1)+4,
\]
\[
(5k+2)(5k+3)=25k(k+1)+6.
\]
Thus each complete block has product congruent to \(4\cdot6=24\equiv-1\pmod{25}\). There are \(18\) complete blocks in \(P(90)\), while \(P(18)\) has three complete blocks followed by \(16,17,18\). Therefore
\[
P(90)\equiv(-1)^{18}=1\pmod{25},
\]
\[
P(18)\equiv(-1)^3(16)(17)(18)
=-4896\equiv4\pmod{25}.
\]
It follows that \(2^{21}M\equiv24\pmod{25}\). Since
\[
2^{10}=1024\equiv-1\pmod{25},
\qquad
2^{21}=2(2^{10})^2\equiv2\pmod{25},
\]
we obtain \(2M\equiv24\pmod{25}\). Because \(2\) and \(25\) have no common factor, this implies \(M\equiv12\pmod{25}\).

The possible last-two-digit endings are therefore \(12,37,62,87\). Since \(M\) is divisible by \(4\), its last two digits must also form a multiple of \(4\). Only \(12\) does. Both digits are nonzero, so \(n=\boxed{12}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
